claims.text: The Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy contains dual nanoprecipitation.
The studied alloy was produced by additive manufacturing.
APT can be integrated with an in situ oxidation heating stage to study the alloy during high-temperature exposure.
High-temperature oxidation induces nanoscale elemental redistribution within the alloy's nanoprecipitates.
Oxidation-induced elemental redistribution leads to the formation of distinct oxide phases.
The distinct oxide phases formed during oxidation correlate with improved oxidation resistance.
Redistribution of key alloying elements within nanoprecipitates facilitates the formation of protective or non-protective oxide phases.
APT can capture near-atomic-scale shifts in the elemental composition of nanoprecipitates.
Near-atomic-scale compositional shifts reveal mechanistic oxidation pathways.
Oxidized nanoprecipitates will exhibit significant nanoscale compositional gradients.
Element-specific depletion or enrichment in nanoprecipitates will be linked to oxide formation.
The oxide phases associated with nanoprecipitate redistribution are responsible for improved oxidation resistance.
The additively manufactured alloy will have improved oxidation resistance relative to conventionally processed counterparts.
Conventional XRD, SEM, and TEM/EDS methods cannot resolve the relevant near-atomic-scale elemental changes during oxidation.
The proposed APT setup can continuously monitor oxidizing samples during in situ heating.
Complementary TEM/EDS can identify the oxide phases correlated with APT compositional maps.
